So, you were at the poster session yesterday afternoon? I did not see you there.
I was there, at the back. While everybody was going to the big posters, I was standing alone with mine.
That always happens in row C. And what were you doing? Just waiting?
I was reading my own abstract again. Then I noticed one man. He was looking at my second figure for a long time.
And you talked to him, of course.
Not immediately. The thing is, he was writing in his notebook, and I did not want to interrupt him.
Interrupt him. That is the whole point of a poster. I was too polite for ten years, and I lost many contacts that way.
In the end I asked him one question, and he stayed for twenty minutes. He works on dosage in leprosy patients.
So while you were being polite, the best contact of the week was standing in front of you.
Exactly. In Bangkok I will not pause. I will say hello while they are still reading.
I was standing at my poster when he asked about the dosage.
While everybody was going to the big posters, I was standing alone with mine.
The thing is, he was writing in his notebook, and I did not want to interrupt.
Then I noticed that she was writing something in her notebook.
I realized I was talking only to one person in the room.

Something happened at my first international congress, and I still tell the story. I was standing at my poster on the second morning, and almost nobody was stopping. Everybody was walking past me towards the big posters at the end of the row. So I was reading my own abstract again, only to look busy. Then I noticed one woman. She was not looking at the whole poster. She was looking at one small figure in the corner, for two or three minutes, and while she was looking, she was writing something in her notebook. The thing is, that was the figure I almost removed the week before. She was from a group in Lisbon, they had the same problem with dosage, and we published together two years later. So my advice is simple. When nobody is stopping, do not pause your work and do not look at the floor. Watch who is looking, and talk to that person.

I want to tell you about the worst five minutes of my professional life, because they became the best. I was presenting in a small room, maybe thirty people, and I was speaking much too fast. While I was explaining my second slide, an older man in the front row was shaking his head. Every time I said a number, he was shaking his head again. I realized I was talking only to him, and I was losing the rest of the room. So I stopped. I paused, I drank some water, and I asked him directly. You disagree. Tell me why. And the reaction of the whole room changed. He was not disagreeing with my data. He was disagreeing with my units. I had milligrams where I needed micrograms. Meanwhile, everybody else was too polite to say it. That man saved my paper. So when you notice a reaction like that, do not continue. Ask.

I was standing at my poster and nobody was stopping. So I was reading my own abstract again, only to look busy. Then I noticed one woman at the corner of my poster. While she was looking, she was writing in her notebook. Two years later we published a paper together.
